title: Pink Eye vs Allergies: How to Tell
summary: Itching usually means allergies. Thick discharge usually means pink eye. Compare symptoms, contagiousness and red flags, and know when to get care.
body_markdown:
Allergies and pink eye can both turn your eyes red, but the pink eye vs allergies difference comes down to two signs.


Allergic eyes can itch intensely, cause your eyes to water, and almost always affect both eyes at once. On the other hand, an infectious pink eye usually starts in one eye and produces a thicker discharge. Eyes itchy? You probably have an allergy. See a thick discharge from your eyes? That’s probably an infection.


Eye allergies are common.[Allergic conjunctivitis affects roughly 10% to 30% of the general population](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK448118/) . If your eyes flare during a high-pollen week, allergy is a reasonable first suspicion.


If your eye looks worse by the hour,[a Circle Medical provider can assess it over a real-time video visit.](https://www.circlemedical.com/online-doctors)


## Pink eye vs allergies at a glance


Here’s five quick checks to see if you have an allergy or pink eye:


- **Itch or discharge:** Intense itching leans allergy, thick discharge leans infection.
- **One eye or both:** Allergy usually hits both eyes at once, infection often starts in one.
- **How fast it came on:** An allergy can flare within minutes of exposure, an infection builds over a day or two.
- **What else is happening:** Sneezing and a runny nose point to allergy, a sore throat or cough points to a virus.
- **Anything urgent:** If you’re experiencing vision changes, eye pain, light sensitivity, or you wear contact lenses, it’s better to see a medical provider today.


If those checks still don’t give you a clear answer, it’s better to look at the full symptom picture.


### Eye allergies vs pink eye: Full symptom comparison


Sign Allergic conjunctivitis (eye allergies) Viral pink eye Bacterial pink eye


**Itching** Intense, the loudest complaint Mild or absent Mild or absent


**Discharge** Clear and watery Watery, sometimes stringy Thick, yellow or green, can seal lids overnight


**One eye or both** Both, almost always Often starts in one, can spread Often one, can spread


**How fast it starts** Minutes to hours after exposure A day or two, often with a cold A day or two


**Pain** None, burning at most None, more of a gritty feeling None to mild


**Contagious** No Yes, highly Yes


**How long it lasts** As long as exposure continues 7 to 14 days, sometimes 2 to 3 weeks Often 2 to 5 days, 2 weeks to fully recover


**Other symptoms** Sneezing, runny nose, itchy throat Sore throat, cough, tender lymph node Usually the eye alone


[The CDC notes that most viral cases of pink eye clear on their own](https://www.cdc.gov/conjunctivitis/about/index.html) . But if your eyes stay red past two weeks, you should see a medical provider.


None of the three conditions normally causes real eye pain. If your eye hurts, that points away from simple conjunctivitis and toward something else.


## The three kinds of pink eye


Conjunctivitis means[inflammation of the membrane covering the white of the eye.](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/pink-eye-conjunctivitis) Three things can set off that inflammation, and each one behaves differently.


### Viral conjunctivitis


[Viruses account for up to 75% of infectious conjunctivitis cases, and adenoviruses cause up to 90% of those](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK470271/) . A viral pink eye often arrives with a cold or a cough.


Observe your eyes during this period. Viral pink eye can cause a watery discharge and start in one eye before reaching the other. Most cases can run 7 to 14 days and clear on its own without medication.


### Bacterial conjunctivitis


Bacteria produce a thicker yellow or green discharge from your eyes, and your eyelids can stick together after sleep. Bacterial pink eye can improve on its own within 2 to 5 days. A medical provider may still prescribe antibiotic eye drops or ointment when clinically appropriate.


[The CDC states clearly that antibiotics will not improve viral pink eye.](https://www.cdc.gov/conjunctivitis/treatment/index.html) Knowing which organism caused the condition changes the treatment plan.


### Allergic conjunctivitis


Allergens set off the same inflammation in your eyes with no germ involved. That is how allergies can cause pink eyes. Your immune system reacts to something harmless, and the eye responds with histamine-driven itching, clear watering, and swelling.


[Pollen, mold spores, dust mites and pet dander](https://aafa.org/allergies/allergy-symptoms/eye-allergy-conjunctivitis/) are usual triggers for allergic conjunctivitis. Symptoms typically appear in both eyes, and the condition cannot be spread to anyone else.


If your eyes react every spring, our post on[allergy season timing](https://www.circlemedical.com/blog-post/when-is-allergy-season) dive deeper into this. Adults can also develop[allergies that start in adulthood](https://www.circlemedical.com/blog-post/adult-onset-allergies-symptoms-causes) , and Circle Medical[treats ongoing seasonal allergy care](https://www.circlemedical.com/blog-post/when-to-see-a-doctor-for-allergies) .


Viruses, bacteria, and allergies can explain why your eyes turned red. But there are other issues that can irritate your eyes that are not conjunctivitis at all.


## What is commonly misdiagnosed as pink eye


Several everyday eye problems can turn the eye red with no virus, bacteria or allergen involved.[Several conditions are regularly mistaken for pink eye](https://www.aao.org/eye-health/tips-prevention/when-pink-eye-is-something-else-conjunctivitis) .


Condition What it feels like What separates it from pink eye


Dry eye Burning, gritty, watery Comes and goes, worse after screen time


Blepharitis Red, crusty, sore lid edges Redness sits on the lash line


Stye One tender lump on the lid Pain has one spot you can point to


Foreign body Sudden scratchy pain in one eye Began at a moment you can name


Contact lens irritation Redness that builds all day Eases an hour after lenses come out


Subconjunctival hemorrhage A bright red patch, no pain Blood-red patch, no discharge


An expensive mistake plenty of people make is treating a stye or dry eye as an infection for a week. A provider can usually sort this out in one visit.


Uveitis and keratitis can threaten vision and need urgent care. For everything else, the practical question is whether what you have can spread to other people.


## Is pink eye contagious?


Viral and bacterial pink eye are contagious. Allergic conjunctivitis is not. It cannot be passed to a partner, a child, or a coworker.


Viral conjunctivitis can stay highly contagious for 10 to 14 days, roughly as long as symptoms last. Bacterial pink eye can spread while the discharge continues, often 2 to 5 days. Treatment can shorten that window when clinically appropriate. Allergic conjunctivitis has no contagious period at all.


Infectious pink eye spreads through hands, shared towels, pillowcases, and eye makeup. Washing your hands often and keeping your towels separate keeps infectious pink eye from spreading throughout your household.


As long as you have no fever and your eye symptoms have been resolved, you can safely return to school or work with your provider’s approval.


## When to see a provider about a red eye


A few symptoms can tell whether you should keep observing your red eye or immediately seek medical attention.


Uveitis or keratitis can cause permanent vision loss when left untreated. Seek care immediately if any of these apply.


1.


Vision changes. Blurring, haze or any loss of sight in the affected eye.


2.


Eye pain. Real pain rather than grittiness, especially deep or aching pain.


3.


Light sensitivity. Photophobia, meaning normal indoor light suddenly hurts.


4.


Injury or a chemical splash. Anything that struck, scratched or splashed the eye.


5.


Contact lens wear. Lens-related infections move fast, so take the lenses out and get the eye assessed.


6.


Symptoms that keep worsening. Redness, pain or discharge building over a couple of days.


7.


Heavy pus with a fever. The CDC lists[intense redness, heavy discharge and fever](https://www.cdc.gov/conjunctivitis/about/index.html) among reasons to seek immediate care.


8.


A newborn with a red eye. Newborns with pink eye symptoms should be seen by a medical provider right away.


## How to get rid of pink eye


Each cause of eye irritation responds to different types of care.


Cause Typical approach Usual timeline


Allergic Reduce the trigger, cool compresses, artificial tears, antihistamine eye drops Can ease hours after leaving the allergen


Viral Supportive care, cool compresses, artificial tears 7 to 14 days, sometimes 2 to 3 weeks


Bacterial Antibiotic eye drops or ointment when clinically appropriate Often 2 to 5 days, 2 weeks to fully recover


Treating an eye allergy starts with getting away from the trigger. That can mean taking a shower after being exposed to pollen, or washing your bedding if you suspect dust mites to be the cause of your red eyes. Cool compresses and artificial tears can bring relief to itchy eyes, and antihistamine eye drops can help as well.


Most viral pink eye clears without antibiotics. Antibiotic eye drops are a prescription decision that a medical provider makes after assessing your condition. Never use medication from someone else.


If a known trigger is behind your symptoms, read about[when allergies need a provider.](https://www.circlemedical.com/blog-post/when-to-see-a-doctor-for-allergies) Talk to a Circle Medical provider today about your symptoms and treatment options.


## Common questions about pink eye and allergies


### How do you rule out pink eye?


You can’t fully rule it out at home, though the signs narrow it fast. Itching in both eyes with clear discharge and no cold symptoms leans allergic. One eye with thick discharge and matted lids leans infectious. A provider settles it by examining the eye and asking about recent exposure.


### Will pink eye from allergies go away on its own?


Allergic conjunctivitis often eases within hours of getting away from the trigger. Symptoms return with each new exposure, so a pollen reaction may last as long as the season. Cool compresses and artificial tears help. If your eyes stay red for weeks, speaking with a primary care provider can help.


### What does the first day of pink eye feel like?


Viral pink eye often begins as grittiness in one eye, like something got in it and won’t rinse out. Redness and watering follow within hours, often alongside a cold. Bacterial pink eye announces itself the next morning with lids sealed by dried discharge. Allergic eyes itch from the first minute.


### Do I have pink eye or is my eye just irritated?


Plain irritation from smoke, chlorine, wind or screen strain usually clears within hours once the cause is gone. Pink eye persists or worsens over a day or two, and it often produces discharge. Redness that eases when your contact lenses come out points toward lens irritation.


### Can allergies cause pink eye in only one eye?


Usually not. Eye allergy typically affects both eyes, since airborne allergens reach both at once. One-sided symptoms can happen when you rub an allergen into a single eye, from pet fur on a hand. A red eye that stays one-sided is more often an infection or a foreign body.


### How long is pink eye contagious for?


Viral conjunctivitis can remain highly contagious for 10 to 14 days, roughly as long as symptoms persist. Bacterial conjunctivitis is contagious while discharge continues, and treatment can shorten that window when clinically appropriate. The CDC advises returning to school or work with a provider’s approval, once fever and symptoms have cleared.


### Do I need antibiotics for pink eye?


Not usually. Most viral pink eye clears without antibiotics, and antibiotics won’t help a viral infection. Bacterial pink eye can improve on its own in 2 to 5 days, though a provider may prescribe antibiotic drops when clinically appropriate. The decision belongs to a provider after an exam.


### Can I wear contacts with pink eye?


You should stop wearing contacts until the eye clears. Lens-related infections can move fast and cause serious damage. Keep the lenses out and get the eye assessed, especially if you woke up with pain, redness or discharge.


## Get your eye looked at today


Your next move depends on what you see in the mirror. Itching in both eyes with clear tears usually means an allergy, so reduce your exposure to the trigger and reach for cool compresses.


One eye with thick discharge usually means an infection, so pause your use of contact lenses, keep your towels separate, and plan on resting for a week or two.


If you’re unsure of which you have, a provider can assess your eye symptoms, when they started, whether one eye or both is affected, what the discharge looks like, and what else you’ve been feeling. Based on that history, they can tell you what to do next: whether it’s reasonable to wait and watch, try allergy relief, or get seen in person sooner. Red flags like vision changes, significant pain, or light sensitivity would point toward an in-person evaluation right away.
